title-group.article-title: Value-based pricing of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone for advanced oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma: a Markov modelling study from the US payer perspective

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: This study aimed to determine the value-based price range at which tislelizumab combined with chemotherapy becomes cost-effective compared with chemotherapy alone for treating advanced oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

sec.title: Design
sec.p: We constructed a three-state Markov model over a lifetime horizon, following the same protocols in the RATIONALE-306 trial. One-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed to assess model robustness.

sec.title: Settings
sec.p: US healthcare system, payer perspective.

sec.title: Primary and secondary outcome measures
sec.p: The primary outcome of the model included value-based per-cycle price of tislelizumab at willingness-to-pay thresholds from US$50 000 to US$200 000 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY). Secondary outcomes were life years and QALY over life-time horizon.

sec.title: Interventions
sec.p: Tislelizumab+chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone followed by second-line paclitaxel in both arms.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Tislelizumab resulted in a gain of 0.543 QALYs (95% CI 0.432 to 0.610) and 0.837 life-years (95% CI 0.780 to 0.915) compared with chemotherapy alone. The value-based price of tislelizumab was determined to be US$1575 to US$7160 per cycle when the willingness to pay threshold was set at US$50 000–US$200 000 per QALY. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the model’s robustness at these price points across various model parameters.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study established a value-based price range for tislelizumab in oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma treatment using robust economic modelling. These findings can be used to guide payers in coverage decisions and inform pricing negotiations for emerging immunotherapies.

caption.title: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY

list-item.p: Individual patient-level age data from the US Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results registry were used to derive the starting age distribution, ensuring the modelled cohort reflects the real-world demographic profile of advanced oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma patients in the USA.

Efficacy inputs were derived from the RATIONALE-306 global phase III randomised controlled trial, and all cost parameters were sourced from 2024 Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services average sales prices and the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, ensuring US-specific economic relevance.

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis with 10 000 Monte Carlo simulations, one-way sensitivity analyses, and scenario analyses for treatment adherence and overall survival HR variations across subpopulations were conducted, demonstrating robustness of the value-based pricing estimates.

Health state utility values were sourced from published economic studies of comparable oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma populations, introducing uncertainty that was addressed through robust sensitivity analyses.

Long-term efficacy beyond trial follow-up was extrapolated using parametric survival models selected by Akaike information criterion and Bayesian information criterion, which introduces uncertainty regarding the durability of treatment effects over a lifetime horizon.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Oesophageal cancer (EC) forms a major public health concern as it ranks as the sixth leading cause of cancer-related mortality in the world. EC is responsible for one in eighteen cancer-related deaths and is associated with approximately 11.7 million disability-adjusted life-years for cases diagnosed between 1990 and 2019 globally, underscoring its substantial impact on health outcomes.1 In the USA, the number of new EC cases is projected to reach 22 070, with an estimated 16 250 deaths in 2025.2 The global economic burden was estimated to be between US$6.6 million and US$10.5 billion annually (up to 0.07% of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in some countries), reflecting the substantial resources required for disease management.3 In the USA, 6 years of Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results (SEER) data showed that among beneficiaries aged 65 and above, annual EC care involved 5275 patients in the initial phase, 5125 in the continuing phase, and 8449 in end-of-life care. With average Medicare (Parts A and B) medical services costs of US$86 500, US$9500 and US$115 300 for these phases, respectively, total annual spending exceeded US$1.1 billion, demonstrating the substantial burden on the healthcare payer.4 5

EC predominantly presents as one of two major histological subtypes: oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and adenocarcinoma. Other less common types include sarcoma, small-cell carcinoma and lymphoma. ESCC prognosis remains poor, with over 75% of patients diagnosed at an advanced or metastatic stage, which results in a 5-year survival rate of approximately 6%.2 6 Current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) treatment guidelines recommend first-line chemotherapy with immunotherapy for patients with PD-L1 combined positive score ≥1. This approach incorporates agents such as cisplatin or oxaliplatin combined with fluoropyrimidine or paclitaxel, administered with programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) inhibitors nivolumab,7 pembrolizumab8 and recently tislelizumab.9 The addition of PD-1 inhibitors to chemotherapy improves the median overall survival (OS) compared with chemotherapy alone. However, most randomised controlled trials (RCTs) used cisplatin and fluorouracil. Alternative regimens such as oxaliplatin or cisplatin in combination with fluoropyrimidine or paclitaxel were studied primarily in Asian populations, limiting broader global applicability. The RATIONALE-306 RCT findings showed that adding tislelizumab to chemotherapy led to a significant increase in median OS to 17.2 months, with an HR of 0.66. Tislelizumab was administered with various chemotherapy combinations, which included NCCN-preferred oxaliplatin or alternatives such as cisplatin combined with a fluoropyrimidine (capecitabine or fluorouracil) or paclitaxel.10

Previous cost-effectiveness analyses of PD-1 treatments for ESCC reported mixed results. For pembrolizumab, two studies found that pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy was not cost-effective in the US setting,11 12 while another analysis suggested borderline cost-effectiveness when applying a willingness-to-pay threshold of US$150 000 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY).13 Prior studies evaluating both nivolumab plus chemotherapy and nivolumab plus chemotherapy/ipilimumab showed that these regimens were not cost-effective for the overall population.14 15 None of these analyses evaluated tislelizumab or included diverse chemotherapy backbones, and at current prices, none of the approved PD-1 inhibitors were found cost-effective in the USA at a willingness-to-pay threshold of US$100 000 per QALY.

In this study, we aimed to determine the cost-effective per-cycle prices of adding tislelizumab to the chemotherapy strategy for the treatment of advanced ESCC for a range of accepted willingness-to-pay thresholds within the US healthcare system.

sec.title: Model overview
sec.p: We developed a three-state Markov model to estimate the price point at which tislelizumab becomes a cost-effective first-line treatment option for managing advanced, unresectable or metastatic ESCC patients. Patients started in the progression-free (PF) state, where the disease is stable, and there is no evidence of disease progression. Patients could either remain PF or transition to a post-progression (PP) state, where patients are still alive with a documented disease progression. This process continued until death, either due to cancer or other causes (ie, background mortality) (figure 1). In the model, two treatment options were compared: (1) tislelizumab (administered for up to 2 years) combined with chemotherapy (oxaliplatin and capecitabine) and (2) chemotherapy alone, followed by second-line paclitaxel therapy for both treatment arms, following the treatment protocol of the RCT. Each model cycle represented 3 weeks, and patients were allowed to transition to the death state at any cycle in the model. The model was implemented in C++, and the statistical analysis was conducted in R. Additional details on model formulation and equations are available in (online supplemental eAppendix 1 in the supplemental material).

caption.title: Markov model structure used to simulate patient transitions through different health states based on the RATIONALE-306 trial. Patients start in the progression-free (PF) state and can remain in the PF or move to post-progression (PP) state for multiple cycles (represented by circular arrows). Transitions between states occur based on probabilities estimated from clinical trial data, with arrows indicating possible transitions between states. The simulation ends when all patients transition to the Death state. Transition probabilities were calculated from parametric survival distributions fitted to RATIONALE-306 trial data.

sec.p: The model inputs included costs, transition probabilities, utilities and adverse event rates for grades three and above (online supplemental eTable 1). The drug and its administration costs were calculated based on 2024 prices. Transition probabilities were calculated from parametric survival distributions fitted to RATIONALE-306 trial’s Kaplan-Meier curves. For each 3-week cycle, the probability of transitioning from PF to PP was derived from progression-free survival (PFS) curves, and the probability of transitioning from PF or PP to Death was derived from OS curves; more details about transition probability calculations are in the supplement materials. The model’s outputs included total costs, life years (LY), QALYs and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). All future costs and QALYs were discounted at an annual rate of 3%. This study followed the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards 2022 guidelines of health economic evaluations.16 The ICERs were compared against willingness-to-pay thresholds ranging from US$50 000 to US$200 000 per QALY. These thresholds reflect those commonly employed in US health economic evaluation, with higher thresholds increasingly accepted for cancer treatments with limited therapeutic alternatives.

sec.title: Patient distribution
sec.p: To estimate the outcomes for patients with ESCC in the USA, we determined the initial age at diagnosis using the age distribution for stage IV EC from the American Joint Committee on Cancer seventh Edition. This information was sourced from SEER data covering the years 2010 to 2015.17

sec.title: Clinical inputs
sec.p: Survival data were obtained from the RATIONALE-306 RCT, using curves for OS and PFS. Data points were extracted using WebPlotDigitizer V.4.6 software.18 We used parametric survival functions: log-logistic models for OS (online supplemental eFigure 1) and PFS (online supplemental eFigure 2) in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm, a log-normal model for OS in the chemotherapy alone arm (online supplemental eFigure 3), and a log-logistic model for PFS in the chemotherapy alone arm (online supplemental eFigure 4). Model fitting was guided by the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC).19 The statistical goodness-of-fit for survival models is summarised in (online supplemental eTable 2), and the fitted model parameters are reported in (online supplemental eTable 3). Adverse event rates were obtained from the RCT for events rated as grade ≥3 and reported in at least 5% of patients. Age-specific background mortality rates were estimated from US life tables.20

Tislelizumab was administered as a 200 mg intravenous infusion on day 1 of each 21-day cycle, in conjunction with chemotherapy regimens according to US guidelines. These regimens included oxaliplatin (130 mg/m²) administered intravenously on day 1 every 3 weeks and capecitabine (1000 mg/m²) administered orally twice daily from days 1 to 14 every 3 weeks. In the control arm placebo was administered intravenously on day 1 of each 21-day cycle, with chemotherapy. After disease progression, patients received paclitaxel. Drug dosages were calculated using a mean body surface area of 1.86 m², based on US population data.21

sec.title: Cost and utility estimates
sec.p: Direct costs included drug costs, administration expenses and management of grade ≥3 adverse events. Drug costs were calculated using the 2024 average sales prices from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).22 Administration costs were calculated from the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule using the Current Procedural Terminology codes.23 Adverse event costs were obtained from a previously published cost-effectiveness analysis with cancer-related events.24 All costs were adjusted to 2024 dollars using the Consumer Price Index calculator.25

Total QALYs were calculated by adjusting survival time with corresponding utility values. Given the absence of direct utility assessment in the RATIONALE-306 study, we used quality of life data for health states and adverse events from published literature with a similar patient population.26 27 Utility values for the PF and PP states were 0.74 and 0.56, respectively.

sec.title: Sensitivity analyses
sec.p: One-way sensitivity analysis was conducted by varying one input parameter at a time within a predefined CI or ±20% of the base-case value. Tislelizumab price was set at US$1575 benchmarking at a willingness to pay (WTP) of US$50 000 per QALY. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was conducted to assess the robustness of our model and address uncertainty in variable estimation. For PSA, cost parameters were assigned a Gamma distribution, which is used for continuous, non-negative, and right-skewed parameters with a lower bound of zero. Probability and utility parameters were assigned a Beta distribution as utilities and probabilities are bounded on the (0, 1) interval. These distribution choices align with International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research recommendations on good research practices. The Gamma and Beta distributions were parameterised using the method of moments, using the mean and SE of each cost input.28 The mean value of each distribution served as the baseline for the base-case result. The SD was set at half of the 95% CI and 20% of the mean for the remaining variables.

Online supplemental eTable 1 presents the model input parameters with baseline values, ranges and assigned distributions. To address uncertainty in utility values, which were obtained from published literature rather than directly measured in the RATIONALE-306 trial, we conducted additional scenario analyses changing PF and PP utility values by 30% from their base-case values. This included one-way sensitivity analyses for each utility independently and a two-way sensitivity analysis varying both utilities at the same time.

The PSA curves presented the probability at which tislelizumab’s incremental cost-effectiveness ratio remains below different WTP thresholds and cost scenarios. Our analysis also investigated the impact of the HR for OS on ICER, comparing treatment with the control groups. The baseline HRs from the RATIONALE-306 trial were 0.66 and 0.62 for OS and PFS, respectively. The explored HRs ranged from 0.45 to 0.95 for OS to determine its effect on ICER by running our model repeatedly while varying tislelizumab costs. This analysis enabled stratification of results by subgroups with different HRs.

We incorporated adherence scenarios into our model to better reflect real-world variability, as treatment adherence affects outcomes and economic evaluation of cancer treatments.29 In RCTs, full adherence is assumed by design, and limited evidence exists quantifying risk reduction associated with partial adherence in cancer patients. Therefore, our base-case analysis assumed full medication adherence for all patients in the treatment arm. We also ran scenarios incorporating a proportion of non-adherent patients in the treatment arm. We explored per-cycle cost of tislelizumab across varying proportions of adherent patients, assuming non-adherent patients experienced no risk reduction.

sec.title: Base-case results
sec.p: For patients with advanced ESCC over the lifetime horizon, the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm yielded an incremental gain of 0.837 life-years (95% CI 0.780 to 0.915), and when adjusted to utility, an incremental gain of 0.543 QALYs (95% CI 0.432 to 0.610) compared with chemotherapy alone. At a WTP benchmark of US$50 000 per QALY, the value-based per-cycle price of tislelizumab was US$1575, corresponding to an ICER of US$49 980 per QALY (95% CI US$43 756 to US$60 915). At US$100 000 per QALY, the value-based price was US$3435, with an ICER of US$99 923 per QALY (95% CI US$86 562 to US$120 850). At US$150 000 per QALY, the value-based price was US$5295, corresponding to an ICER of US$149 865 per QALY (95% CI US$129 316 to US$180 854). At the highest threshold of US$200 000 per QALY, the price increased to US$7160, with an ICER of US$199 942 per QALY (95% CI US$171 144 to US$240 972). Full results are presented in table 1.

caption.title: Base-case results for adding tislelizumab to chemotherapy across different tislelizumab cost scenarios

sec.title: Sensitivity analyses
sec.p: The one-way sensitivity analysis assumed that tislelizumab was priced at the base-case value of US$1575 for a WTP of US$50 000 per QALY. The most influential parameters in the model were tislelizumab price and the utilities of the PF and PP health states (online supplemental eFigure 5). Chemotherapy drug and second-line paclitaxel treatment costs had a negligible influence on the ICER, with parameter variations producing changes of less than US$200 per QALY from the base case. This finding is consistent with the model structure, in which both treatment arms share identical chemotherapy regimens, causing chemotherapy costs to largely cancel out in the incremental cost calculation, with the differential cost driven almost entirely by tislelizumab. Administration costs and adverse event incidence rates demonstrated intermediate sensitivity, remaining well below the US$50 000 per QALY threshold across all parameter ranges tested.

We conducted one-way and two-way sensitivity analyses, varying PF and PP health-state utilities by 30% from their base-case values, testing a wider range than the 20% used in the primary one-way sensitivity analysis at a US$50 000 WTP threshold. In the one-way analysis of PF utility (online supplemental eTable 4), varying this parameter from 0.518 to 0.962 produced ICERs ranging from US$57 866 to US$43 914 per QALY, with corresponding value-based prices of US$1320 and US$1830 per cycle, respectively. In the one-way analysis of PP utility (online supplemental eTable 5), varying this parameter from 0.392 to 0.728 produced ICERs of US$59 127 to US$43 215 per QALY, with value-based prices of US$1285 and US$1865 per cycle. In the two-way sensitivity analysis, we simultaneously varied both utilities by 30% (online supplemental eTable 6). The ICER ranged from US$38 660 to US$70 491 per QALY, and the value-based price at a US$50 000 WTP threshold ranged from US$2120 to US$1030 per cycle. The results show that utility values were not the primary driver of value-based pricing. ICERs from one-way sensitivity analyses aligned with the CI (US$43 756 to US$60 915 per QALY), indicating consistency between deterministic and probabilistic uncertainty. The wider range in the two-way analysis reflects an extreme scenario, yet ICERs remained below the US$100 000 WTP threshold.

Figure 2 illustrates the cost-effectiveness acceptability curves, at varying WTP thresholds (US$50–200K/QALY) and multiple per-cycle prices. The figure shows the probability of cost-effectiveness. The analysis revealed a high probability that the tislelizumab arm would remain cost-effective at a lower per-cycle price across all WTP thresholds. For example, when per-cycle costs were below US$1500 for an ICER of US$50 000 per QALY, tislelizumab had more than 95% probability of being cost-effective. At the US$100 000/QALY threshold, 100% probability of cost-effectiveness was maintained up to approximately US$3000 per cycle, crossing the 90% probability reference line at approximately US$3500 per cycle before declining to near zero by US$5000 per cycle. At the US$150 000/QALY threshold, tislelizumab maintained 100% probability up to approximately US$5500 per cycle, declining to near zero by US$7000 per cycle. At the US$200 000/QALY threshold, 100% probability was sustained up to approximately US$7000 per cycle, with the probability declining toward zero only beyond US$9500 per cycle. As the WTP threshold increased, tislelizumab maintained a high probability of cost-effectiveness at higher per-cycle costs. Across all WTP thresholds, the curves exhibit a consistent pattern, confirming that the value-based prices reported in table 1 represent robust and reliable boundaries at which tislelizumab achieves acceptable cost-effectiveness under parameter uncertainty.

caption.title: Cost-effectiveness curves with a varying willingness to pay for different prices of tislelizumab. The curves show the probability of tislelizumab being cost-effective as its price changes, with WTP thresholds of US$50 000, US$100 000, US$150 000 and US$200 000 per QALY gained. The red dotted line in the figure represents a 90% probability of tislelizumab being cost-effective at various price points. ICER, incremental cost-effectiveness ratio; QALY, quality-adjusted life-year; WTP, willingness to pay.

sec.p: Figure 3 illustrates ICER values for tislelizumab at varying per-cycle prices across different OS HRs. Each panel represents a distinct HR. With HRs ranging from 0.45 to 0.95, ICERs remained below US$200 000 per QALY at different tislelizumab costs. The plots showed linear increases in ICER with rising per-cycle costs, demonstrating how changes in OS HR affected tislelizumab cost-effectiveness. To address subgroup-specific pricing, we mapped prespecified subgroup OS HRs from the RATIONALE-306 trial to the HR scenario analyses, at a US$50 000 WTP threshold. Results are summarised across four subgroup dimensions: for age, patients ≥65 years (HR 0.62) had a higher value-based price (US$2000/cycle) than those <65 years (HR 0.73, US$1280/cycle). For geography, Japanese patients showed the most favourable HR (0.49, US$3300/cycle), followed by non-Asian regions (HR 0.66, ~US$1680/cycle) and Asian patients excluding Japan (HR 0.70, US$1440/cycle). For race, White patients (HR 0.61) corresponded to US$2090/cycle versus Asian and other races (HR 0.69, US$1490/cycle). For chemotherapy backbone, platinum-fluoropyrimidine (HR 0.66) corresponded to US$1680/cycle and platinum-paclitaxel (HR 0.69) to US$1490/cycle. Treatment adherence rates affected acceptable tislelizumab pricing (online supplemental eFigure 6). Assuming a fixed ICER threshold of US$50 000 per QALY, as the proportion of adherent patients increased from 50% to 100%, per-cycle tislelizumab costs rose from US$904 to US$1575. This represented a 74% increase in value-based price across the full adherence range, reflecting a linear and consistent relationship between adherence and acceptable pricing. At every 10% increment in adherence, the value-based price increased by approximately US$134 per cycle on average, from US$904 at 50% adherence, to US$1060 at 60%, US$1206 at 70%, US$1335 at 80% and US$1475 at 90% adherence. Thus, adherence to medication could potentially affect health outcomes and, as a result, affect the price, underscoring the importance of adherence support interventions in maximising the economic value of tislelizumab.

caption.title: ICER for variation of cost of tislelizumab at different overall survival HRs. Each panel represents a different overall survival HR, ranging from 0.45 to 0.95. The HR measures the effect of tislelizumab on survival, with lower values indicating better survival outcomes, note that the base-case of overall survival HR is 0.66. ICER, incremental cost-effectiveness ratio; QALY, quality-adjusted life-year.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The addition of PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors to chemotherapy demonstrated significant efficacy in cancer management. However, accessing approved PD-1 therapies has considerable financial implications and poses a substantial burden for patients and healthcare payers worldwide. In the USA, uniform pricing models exacerbate this economic pressure by pricing new therapies on their initial approved indication; thus, new approved therapies for the ESCC setting inherit high prices established by their earlier approvals in other cancers.

Previous cost-effectiveness analyses of Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved PD-1 inhibitors in advanced ESCC showed that none were cost-effective in the US setting at a US$100 000 per QALY threshold, and some are marginally cost-effective at US$150 000 per QALY.1115 Some economic evaluations employed network meta-analyses to indirectly compare PD-1 inhibitors by anchoring to a placebo arm, suggesting that tislelizumab provided greater QALY gains than pembrolizumab or nivolumab.30 31 Other network meta-analyses also indicated that tislelizumab was associated with improved OS compared with pembrolizumab and nivolumab.3234 However, these analyses produced wide CIs, and head-to-head comparisons cannot be reliably inferred from indirect evidence. Therefore, this analysis focused on a more robust strategy by replicating the RATIONALE-306 trial design and inferring the initial age distribution from US patients to directly compare tislelizumab plus chemotherapy against chemotherapy alone across multiple guideline-supported backbones, preserving internal validity and avoiding indirect comparisons limitations. Current US pricing provides important context for our value-based pricing analysis. Pembrolizumab costs approximately US$11 146 per cycle, and nivolumab costs US$7620 per cycle for ESCC treatment.22 Based on recent market entry data, tislelizumab might be priced at approximately US$10 031 per cycle (representing a 10% discount to pembrolizumab).35 At the upper bound of our value-based range (US$7160/cycle), tislelizumab would be priced approximately 36% lower than pembrolizumab and 6% lower than nivolumab, potentially enhancing formulary positioning and payer coverage decisions specifically as a first-line treatment. However, our modelling demonstrates that tislelizumab at its anticipated market price of US$10 031 per cycle would not achieve cost-effectiveness for the overall population at any conventional willingness-to-pay threshold. The gap between this price and the value-based ceiling (US$7160/cycle at a US$200 000/QALY threshold) has a direct implication for patient access, particularly for uninsured and underinsured populations facing high out-of-pocket costs. Pricing within the value-based range could improve patient access by reducing cost-sharing and potentially expanding coverage through preferred formulary selection. From a market competition perspective, value-based pricing could position tislelizumab as a cost-effective alternative.

Our base-case analysis used pooled RATIONALE-306 population data without stratification by geographic region, patient race, or any other subgroup. The trial reported variation in outcomes across geographic-based subgroups, with HRs of OS of 0.49 in patients from Japan to 0.70 in patients from other Asian countries. Separate race-based analyses showed HRs of 0.69 for Asian and other races compared with 0.61 for White patients. These subgroup differences in treatment effect also have implications for value-based pricing across patient populations. Stronger survival benefits in certain subgroups could position tislelizumab at a higher value-based price, further supporting its competitive positioning relative to current first-line treatments. Our scenario analyses varying OS HRs (figure 3) provided value-based pricing estimates that reflected this population heterogeneity documented in the trial.

This economic evaluation has several limitations. First, the absence of extended follow-up data of the trial participants might have introduced uncertainty about projected outcomes. To mitigate the potential bias, we simulated the model with a life-time horizon and used survival estimates from the published trial survival curves. Second, we did not consider the cost of supportive and end-of-life care. Third, we used the utility estimates for health states and adverse events from previous economic studies, as the RCT of tislelizumab lacked health state utility data. To validate our findings, we performed sensitivity analyses, adjusting all variables by 20% and additionally tested wider uncertainty ranges for health state utilities by varying them by 30% (online supplemental eTables 4-6). Fourth, in our analysis, we used generic pricing for the NCCN-preferred oxaliplatin chemotherapy backbone and second-line paclitaxel. Since both treatment arms were assumed to have identical chemotherapy regimens, chemotherapy costs cancel out in the incremental cost-effectiveness calculation, so the differential cost will be entirely due to the additional per-cycle treatment of tislelizumab. Therefore, using alternative regimens does not change the incremental costs, ICER, or value-based pricing thresholds. Despite these limitations, this research offered valuable insights for policymakers and healthcare professionals regarding tislelizumab cost-effectiveness across a range of WTP thresholds and patient populations. In conclusion, this study determined the economic value of adding tislelizumab to the chemotherapy regimen in the context of the US healthcare system for patients with advanced, unresectable, or metastatic oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

sec.title: Data availability statement
sec.p: All data used in this research are publicly available and non-proprietary. Data sources include published clinical trial results (RATIONALE-306), Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services pricing databases, US life tables, and published literature. The economic model and analysis code are available from the corresponding author upon request.
